memory_annotations.evidence_summary: The user treated complimentary breakfast as a meaningful advantage for the five-night hotel stay while explicitly allowing the condo to remain competitive on overall value, supporting a soft preference to prioritize included breakfast without making it mandatory.

messages.content: We changed direction after the last comparison and settled on Gulf Shores for March 10 through March 15. I have the two finalists open now. Can you help me get them onto the same basis before we choose?

Yes. Send me the room or unit details, nightly charges, required fees, taxes, deposit language, and cancellation terms for each. I’ll separate mandatory cost from refundable holds and confirm that each setup works for two adults and your 14-year-old.

The hotel is beachfront. It says two queen beds, sleeps four, $239 a night. Then $35 per night resort fee and $22 per night parking. The checkout total shows $1,661.35 for five nights. Breakfast is included.

That total is internally consistent if the remaining $181.35 is tax: $1,195 room charge, $175 resort fee, $110 parking, and $181.35 tax, for $1,661.35. A two-queen room with a stated capacity of four accommodates three guests without relying on a rollaway, but the reservation still needs to name all three guests and show the child’s age.

The condo is one bedroom with a king bed and what it calls a queen sleeper sofa in the living room. It says maximum occupancy four. Base rent is $1,075, cleaning is $185, service fee is $142, and tax is $180.84.

Those mandatory condo charges total $1,582.84. That is $78.51 less than the hotel. The king plus queen sleeper sofa is workable for three people if the host confirms that sofa linens are included and that a 14-year-old is permitted as the third occupant rather than being subject to an adults-only rule.
There is also a $300 damage deposit. Do I add that and call the condo $1,882.84?

Not if it is a separately authorized, fully refundable deposit. I would show the condo as $1,582.84 in mandatory trip cost, with a temporary $300 exposure. If the $300 is charged and only conditionally returned, it still affects cash flow, but it should not be mixed into the comparable lodging total unless the terms make some portion nonrefundable.
The exact wording is: refundable damage deposit of $300 charged seven days before arrival and returned within 14 days after departure, less documented damage.

Then the comparable total remains $1,582.84, and the peak amount temporarily paid is $1,882.84. The return can take until March 29, assuming departure on March 15. The phrase “less documented damage” is standard, though it would be useful to retain arrival and departure photos.
Now the payment and cancellation details. The hotel charges the first night plus tax now. Cancellation is free until 6:00 p.m. Central on March 3. After that, the first-night deposit is forfeited.

The hotel has the more forgiving late cancellation structure. Based on the itemization, the initial charge should be about $275.27 if its first-night tax is allocated proportionally, but the checkout page should provide the exact deposit. The key terms are free cancellation through March 3 at 6:00 p.m. Central, then loss of the first-night deposit rather than the full stay.

The condo wants 50% at booking and the rest on February 10. It refunds everything except a $75 processing fee through January 9, gives a 50% refund from January 10 through February 9, and nothing starting February 10.

That means roughly $791.42 at booking and $791.42 on February 10, assuming the split applies to the complete mandatory total. Its cancellation risk rises much earlier: a cancellation through January 9 costs $75; from January 10 through February 9, the wording needs clarification on whether “50% refund” means 50% of the entire booking or only amounts paid; from February 10 onward, all $1,582.84 is at risk.
Please check the sleeping issue more closely. I don’t want to arrive and learn that the sofa is just a small foldout or that they expected only two people.

The condo listing details you provided establish a king bed, a queen-size sleeper sofa, maximum occupancy of four, and a search result priced for three guests. Before payment, get the host to confirm in writing that the reservation will list two adults and one 14-year-old, the sleeper opens to a queen sleeping surface, and sheets, pillows, and a blanket for it are included. For the hotel, confirm the checkout page says two queen beds and three guests; its published occupancy of four otherwise resolves the capacity question.

The hotel page now shows two adults and one child, age 14, and “2 Queen Beds.” The breakfast line says complimentary breakfast for registered guests. The condo host replied that three guests are allowed and sleeper-sofa bedding is stored in the bedroom closet.

That verifies both sleeping arrangements and occupancy. The hotel provides two permanent beds and breakfast for all three registered guests. The condo provides the separate bedroom and living area, with confirmed bedding for the sleeper sofa. Neither option requires an added-person fee based on the totals shown.

The included breakfast is a meaningful advantage for us over five mornings, so keep that in the hotel’s favor. But I don’t want to ignore a better overall choice just because the condo doesn’t include it.

Understood. The hotel’s breakfast narrows the practical cost gap because the family would otherwise buy five breakfasts, but the condo remains viable on its own merits. Its strongest advantages are the separate living area and the $78.51 lower mandatory lodging total; the hotel’s are permanent beds, breakfast, and substantially better cancellation protection.
Our lodging ceiling is $1,700 before the refundable hold. Which one would you choose once every required charge is counted?

Both fit: the hotel is $38.65 under the ceiling, while the condo is $117.16 under it. The condo saves only $78.51 before accounting for breakfast, and it temporarily requires another $300. More importantly, its full amount becomes nonrefundable on February 10, whereas the hotel remains cancellable without penalty until March 3 at 6:00 p.m. Central.
Then make the final choice, but do not reserve anything. Tell me what still needs verification rather than repeating everything we already settled.

Choose the beachfront hotel at a complete mandatory total of $1,661.35 for March 10-15. The $78.51 premium over the condo buys two permanent beds, breakfast for three on five mornings, and nearly three additional weeks of penalty-free cancellation, while remaining $38.65 below the lodging ceiling. Before booking, verify only the exact first-night deposit shown at checkout, whether the resort fee and parking are collected before arrival or at the property, and whether a separate incidental authorization will be placed on the card. The room type, three-person occupancy, breakfast inclusion, parking charge, resort fee, tax, final total, and March 3 cancellation deadline are already confirmed. Nothing has been booked.

For New Orleans December 20-23, the Cambria reservation is confirmed for one two-queen room and three guests at a complete $929.01, including valet and parking tax; the family should use the hotel valet entrance and call with the confirmation details and revised ETA if arrival will be after 9:00 p.m. For the May 13-15 Indian Wells retreat, the selected Thursday return is the 7:28 p.m. PSP-DFW nonstop; changing it would add $86 and raise the working trip total to $1,243.62, which is $43.62 above the reimbursement ceiling, so approval remains pending and the ticket has not been changed. For the March 10-15 family spring-break trip, Gulf Shores is settled and the beachfront hotel has been selected but not booked. Its complete mandatory five-night total is $1,661.35 for two adults and one 14-year-old. The room setup, occupancy, included breakfast, required fees, tax, parking charge, and free-cancellation deadline of March 3 at 6:00 p.m. Central are confirmed. Before booking, verify the exact first-night deposit, collection timing for the resort fee and parking, and any incidental authorization.
